question: Investigate remembered encounter and pronouns, brother versus חביבך, and later unnamed speaker. Capture the competing rain date third of Marheshvan and narrated precedent. Use translations and commentaries to distinguish certainty from conjecture.
scope_checked: Read: JT Taanit 1:1-1:3 (Guggenheimer Hebrew + English with notes; Venice; Mechon-Mamre; Schwab French for 1:2); commentaries on 1:2:4 available on Sefaria (Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah, Mareh HaPanim, Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael, Ohr LaYesharim), Penei Moshe and Korban HaEdah on 1:2:5 and 1:3:1; parallels JT Megillah 3:7:3, JT Shabbat 1:2, JT Sanhedrin 10:1, JT Shekalim 6:2:6 and 7:2:9, Bavli Taanit 3a and 4b; quoting commentaries (Tosefta Kifshutah Terumot 5:10, Lieberman's Sifrei Zuta study §79, Mishnat Eretz Yisrael); lexicon entries (Jastrow חביב, צות/צית, בולי, נהר; A Dictionary of the Talmud צית). Not checked: manuscripts directly (Leiden, Escorial), Guggenheimer's Megillah/Shabbat printed introductions, Sheyarei Korban (request returned 404; this does not show that it has nothing on the passage), Ridbaz, Sefer Nir, Lieberman's Yerushalmi Kifshuto. The Sefaria Community Translation returned no text for 1:2; that says nothing about whether other translations exist.

findings.claim: The halakhah opens with an unnamed plural group asking a question 'before him', and 'he' answers 'them': practice is that where one mentions rain one also asks for it. The text names neither the askers nor the one who answers.

evidence.exact_quote: בעון קומוי או נימר כאן להזכיר כאן לשאלה אמר לון הלכה מקום שמזכירין שואלין
They asked before him

findings.reasoning: בעון is a 3rd-person plural verb ('they asked'). קומוי is 'before him'. אמר לון is 'he said to them'. None of these has a named antecedent in the segment. (My translation: 'They asked before him: or should we say, here it is about mentioning and there about asking? He said to them: the practice is that where one mentions, one asks.')
findings.graph_effect: Keep the askers as an unnamed group node. Keep the answerer as a pronoun mention until coreference is resolved (see F2).

findings.claim: Every consulted commentary that comments on this phrase (Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah, Ohr LaYesharim), and both translations, take 'him' (the one asked, who then answers) to be R. Yohanan. The text also supports this: two lines later, R. Hiyya bar Ba brings the same formula from Tyre in R. Yohanan's name.

evidence.exact_quote: דר' יוחנן או דילמא נימר דכאן ברישא דהמתני' להזכיר
הקשו לפני רבי יוחנן
שאלו לפניו (לפני רבי יוחנן)
R. Joḥanan.
fut-il demandé à R. Yohanan
רבי חייה בר בא אתא מן צור ואמר מן שמיה דרבי יוחנן הלכה מקום שמזכירין שואלין

findings.reasoning: R. Yohanan is the last named authority in 1:2:2-1:2:3. The same halakhic formula is later brought explicitly in his name, so the commentators' identification fits the text. It is still a coreference reading, not an explicit naming.
findings.graph_effect: Link the opening answerer to R. Yohanan, with basis = commentary consensus plus internal support (not 'explicit'). The askers stay unnamed. Do not identify them with R. Yose and R. Hananya, whose remembered scene is a separate report.

findings.claim: As printed, R. Yose addresses 'R. Hananya the brother of Rav Hoshaya' (אחוי דרב הושעיה). In the same sentence he calls the shop owner 'Rav Hoshaya חביבך'.

evidence.exact_quote: א"ר יוסה לרבי חנניה אחוי דרב הושעיה נהיר את כד הוינן קיימין קומי חנותיה דרב הושעיה חביבך
אמר רבי יוסה לרבי חנייה אחוי דרב הושעיה נהיר את כד הוינן קיימין קומי חנותיה דרב הושעיה חביבך
dost thou remember when we were standing &c.?

findings.reasoning: Venice and Mechon-Mamre agree on אחוי ('his brother'). Mechon-Mamre spells the addressee חנייה. נהיר את = 'do you remember' (Jastrow).
findings.graph_effect: Record the printed epithet 'brother of Rav Hoshaya' as a textual reading only (see F5-F6 for why it should not become a sibling edge).

findings.claim: חביב has two lexical senses: 'beloved' and 'uncle, father's brother'. Every interpreter consulted takes the uncle sense here: Korban HaEdah and Ohr LaYesharim (דודך), Guggenheimer ('your uncle'), Schwab ('ton oncle').

evidence.exact_quote: uncle, father’s brother
beloved, dear, precious; favored, privileged.
זכור אתה כשהיינו עומדין לפני חנותו של ר"ה דודך
כאשר היינו עומדים לפני חנותו של רב הושעיה דודך
do you remember when we were standing in front of your uncle Rav Hoshaia’s store
devant la boutique de R. Oshia ton oncle

findings.reasoning: The 'beloved' sense is lexically possible, but none of the commentaries or translations I checked adopts it for this line. It stays a live lexical option with no interpretive support in the checked sources.
findings.graph_effect: Treat the 'uncle' reading as primary. Keep 'beloved' as a low-support alternative branch.

findings.claim: Two parallel Yerushalmi passages give Hananya's epithet as 'son of the brother of Rav Hoshaya'. JT Megillah 3:7:3 repeats almost the same remembered scene at Rav Hoshaya's shop and uses both בר אחוי and חביבך.

evidence.exact_quote: לְרִבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר אָחוֹי דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָה. נָהִיר אַתְּ כַּד דַּהֲוִינָן קַיָימִין קֳדָם חָנוּתָה דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָה חָבִיבָךְ
said to Rebbi Ḥanania the son of Rav Hoshaia’s brother, do you remember when we were standing in front of your uncle’s store
רבי חנניה בן אחוי דרב הושעיה אמר מתניתין בעמי הארץ
Rebbi Ḥananiah the son of Rav Hoshaia’s brother

findings.reasoning: In Megillah the full epithet and חביבך occur together without contradiction. That suggests the Taanit reading אחוי is short by one word (בר). In Megillah the speaker is printed as bare רבי (Guggenheimer n.150 cites Soferim 13:4 with a different speaker), and the sage who passes is R. Abba bar Zavda. So the Megillah scene is a parallel formula, not proof that the same event is meant.
findings.graph_effect: This supports a nephew relation through an unnamed parent. Do not merge the Megillah and Taanit scenes into one event.

findings.claim: Guggenheimer and Ohr LaYesharim both emend the Taanit text to 'son of Rav Hoshaya's brother'. On that reading Hananya is Rav Hoshaya's nephew, and the Hoshaya in his epithet and the shop owner are the same person. Read literally, 'brother of Rav Hoshaya' plus 'your uncle Rav Hoshaya' cannot both describe one Hoshaya. No source I checked proposes two different Hoshayas here. Schwab translates both phrases literally and does not comment.

evidence.exact_quote: From the following it is obvious that one has to read “son of Rav Hoshaia’s brother”
(צריך לומר: בר אחוי)
בן אחיו של רב הושעיה (אמורא בדור השלישי)
R. Yossé dit à R. Hanina, frère de R. Oshia: tu te souviens

findings.reasoning: The emendation rests on three things: the internal contradiction, the lexical sense 'father's brother', and the parallels in F5. It remains an emendation of the printed text.
findings.graph_effect: Replace the explicit sibling_of(Hananya, Rav Hoshaya) with: child_of(Hananya, unnamed parent) plus sibling_of(unnamed parent, Rav Hoshaya), both with basis = emendation/commentary. Make the two Rav Hoshaya mentions one entity under this branch. Keep the printed 'brother' as a rejected/variant reading, not as an asserted edge.

findings.claim: Lieberman identifies the shop owner as 'R. Hoshaya the second', who had a shop in Tiberias. He cites this passage and JT Megillah 3. JT Sanhedrin 10:1 has 'the Tiberians' measuring distance 'up to the shop of R. Hoshaya'. Ohr LaYesharim places Rav Hoshaya in the third Amoraic generation.

evidence.exact_quote: והוא ר' הושעיה השני שהיתה לו חנות בטבריא, כמפורש בירושלמי תענית פ"א ה"ב
טִיבֵּרִיאֵי אָמְרִין. מִן סִידְרָא רַבָּה עַד חָנוּתֵיהּ דְרִבִּי הוֹשַׁעְיָה
בן אחיו של רב הושעיה (אמורא בדור השלישי)

findings.reasoning: This is scholarly historical identification. The Sanhedrin passage spells the name רבי הושעיה, not רב, and gives no kinship. Placing the shop in Tiberias is an inference that joins passages, not a statement in Taanit. The same chapter (JT Taanit 1:3:2) also has a ruling 'in the name of R. Hoshaya' that should not be merged by name alone.
findings.graph_effect: At most, add an optional historical-identity hypothesis (shop owner = 'R. Hoshaya II', Tiberias) with basis = modern scholarship. Do not attach a place edge from Taanit alone. Do not merge with other Hoshaya mentions by name.

findings.claim: 'We' in the remembered scene (הוינן 'we were', שאלנן 'we asked') includes at least R. Yose, the speaker, and very likely R. Hananya: Yose asks him to remember the scene, and at the end speaks of Hananya's own action ('you ...'). The text does not say whether anyone else was present.

evidence.exact_quote: נהיר את כד הוינן קיימין
עבר רבי זעורה ושאלנן ליה ואמר עוד אנא היא צריכה לי עבר רבי יסא ושאלנן ליה ואמר עוד אנא היא צריכה לי
ושאלנו ליה ואמר גם לדידי קמיבעיא לי

findings.reasoning: Asking the addressee whether he remembers presupposes he was there. The plural verb does not limit the group to two. The whole scene is Yose's recollection inside the halakhah, so it has the status of reported speech.
findings.graph_effect: Participation edges for Yose (high) and Hananya (medium-high). Give them voice = R. Yose (reported recollection), not narrator. The unnamed parent and Rav Hoshaya are not participants, only the owner of the landmark.

findings.claim: R. Zeura and then R. Yasa each passed by, were asked, and replied 'עוד אנא היא צריכה לי'. Commentators read עוד two ways: 'still' (Penei Moshe, Guggenheimer) or 'I too' (Korban HaEdah, Ohr LaYesharim). Either way, each sage says he is himself unsure.

evidence.exact_quote: עדיין אני מסופק בדבר זה אם יש לחלק בין הזכרה לבין שאלה
גם לדידי קמיבעיא לי
this is still problematic for me

findings.reasoning: The 'I too' reading implies the questioners were also unsure. The 'still' reading implies an ongoing doubt. Neither changes who spoke.
findings.graph_effect: asks(Yose+Hananya → Zeura), asks(Yose+Hananya → Yasa), answers-with-doubt from each. These stay inside R. Yose's recollection.

findings.claim: Interpreters differ on what exactly the two sages were asked. Penei Moshe and Ohr LaYesharim say it was whether mentioning rain and asking for rain can be separated (the 'או נימר' question). Guggenheimer says it was the best date to start praying for rain.

evidence.exact_quote: אם יש לחלק בין הזכרה לבין שאלה
The date when best to start praying for rain.

findings.reasoning: The text only says 'we asked him'. The content has to be supplied from context. The two readings are close: Guggenheimer's n.113 connects the mention/request rule to the autumn start date.
findings.graph_effect: The content role of the asks edges should point to the mention-vs-request question, noting Guggenheimer's start-date reading as an alternative.

findings.claim: 'ובסופה את מציית ליה ואמר לא שנייא' is read in three ways. (a) 'At the end you made him listen / pressed him, and he said...': Jastrow, A Dictionary of the Talmud, Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah ('you cried out with him in argument'), Schwab. (b) 'At the end you heard from him': Guggenheimer. (c) Emend to one word אתמציית, 'at the end it became clear to him': Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael (R. Z. W. Rabinovitz), endorsed by Lieberman and followed by Ohr LaYesharim. On (a) and (b) Hananya takes part in the final exchange. On (c) he does not.

evidence.exact_quote: and finally thou madest him listen (to thee), and he said &c.
פַעל, גרם להקשבה ולציות
to cause to listen
שלחצת אותו לומר לך האמת
ולבסוף אתה צעקת עמו דרך פלפול
Ce n’est qu’après l’avoir poussé à bout et pressé, qu’il finit par s’écrier
But at the end you heard from him: there is no difference; where one mentions one asks.
פי' שזכר ונמצא לו דין זה, ומלת "אתמציית" נתחלקה לשתים
כלומר ובסוף נתמצתה לו [ההלכה] ואמר וכו'
ובסוף נמצאה לו (נודעה ונתבררה לרבי אסי שאלה זו), שידע להשיב עליה

findings.reasoning: Both printed Hebrew texts have two words, את מציית. Reading (c) is a conjectural emendation, though highly regarded (Lieberman calls it 'הגהתו היפה', 'his fine emendation'). Reading (b) is the most neutral translation and treats the clause as transmission. Reading (a) treats it as a pressured exchange.
findings.graph_effect: Branch the final exchange. (a) speech: Hananya presses the sage, and the sage answers; (b) transmission: Hananya hears the ruling from the sage; (c) the sage comes to know the ruling himself and states it (no Hananya edge). The earlier single heard_from edge is branch (b) only.

findings.claim: The pronoun 'him' (ליה), the one who finally says 'לא שנייא', is not named. The nearest antecedent is R. Yasa. Ohr LaYesharim names him outright ('R. Assi'), and Schwab's French continues from R. Yassa. No consulted source makes it R. Zeura.

evidence.exact_quote: ובסוף נמצאה לו (נודעה ונתבררה לרבי אסי שאלה זו)
עבר רבי יסא (רבי אסי, אמורא ארץ ישראלי בדור השלישי)
et la même question ayant été adressée à R. Yassa qui passa, il y répondit de même
ולרבי אסי היו דברי רבי יוחנן ברורים, ולרבי זירא היו הדברים מסופקים.
אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא לְרַבִּי אַסִּי: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי?

findings.reasoning: Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah, Guggenheimer and Jastrow leave 'him' unnamed. Ohr LaYesharim supports R. Yasa by linking to Bavli Taanit 4b, where R. Assi transmits R. Yohanan and R. Zeira questions him. That is cross-text support, and it depends on identifying Yerushalmi יסא with Bavli אסי, which is a commentator's identification, not something the text states.
findings.graph_effect: Resolve the final speaker to R. Yasa at medium confidence (basis: nearest antecedent plus one commentary). Zeura is a low-confidence alternative. Do not create a Yasa–Yohanan transmission edge from this Yerushalmi passage: Yasa is not said to cite Yohanan here.

findings.claim: R. Hiyya bar Ba came from Tyre and said the ruling in R. Yohanan's name. Ohr LaYesharim suggests, explicitly as a possibility, that he had heard it from R. Yohanan in Tyre.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי חייה בר בא אתא מן צור ואמר מן שמיה דרבי יוחנן
אפשר, שכשחזר רבי חייא בר אבא מצור, אמר משמו של רבי יוחנן מה ששמע ממנו בצור.

findings.reasoning: The travel and the attribution are textual. The claim that R. Yohanan was in Tyre, and that the ruling was heard there, is marked 'אפשר' ('it is possible') by the commentator. It is conjecture.
findings.graph_effect: reports_in_name_of(Hiyya bar Ba → Yohanan) and origin = Tyre stay explicit. Do not add co-location of Yohanan in Tyre.

findings.claim: R. Aha preached in the study house and R. Yirmeya in the 'כנישתא דבולי'. The ruling formula follows once, after both clauses. Ohr LaYesharim says both preached R. Yohanan's ruling. What בולי means is disputed: a place called Buli (Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah), 'importance' (Penei Moshe's alternative), the city council (Guggenheimer; Ohr LaYesharim, which conjectures Tiberias), or 'prob.' the senate building in Sepphoris (Jastrow).

evidence.exact_quote: רבי אחא דרש בבית מדרשא רבי ירמיה דרש בכנישתא דבולי הלכה מקום שמזכירין שואלין
שניהם דרשו כדברי רבי יוחנן
מקום הנקרא בולי. א"נ בולי לשון חשיבות הוא
בבית הכנסת של עיר בולי
prob. the assembly building of the Senate in Sepphoris
כנראה נערכו בבית הכנסת של הבולי בטבריה כינוסי מועצת העיר
נוּקְנִיקָה אִישְׁתַּכַּח בִּכְנִישְׁתָּא דְבוּלֵי. אֲתַא עוֹבְדָא קוֹמֵי רִבִּי יִרְמְיָה.

findings.reasoning: The two preachings are separate events in separate places. Saying they share the same content is a reasonable syntactic reading. JT Shekalim 7:2 connects a case in the same synagogue with R. Yirmeya, but that is a co-occurrence, not evidence of where the building was.
findings.graph_effect: Two public-teaching events. Content = the mention/request ruling (medium-high). The place 'כנישתא דבולי' has no fixed city: Sepphoris (Jastrow) and Tiberias (Ohr LaYesharim) are both hedged conjectures.

findings.claim: The competing dates come from the Mishnah (JT 1:3:1 / Mishnah Taanit 1:3). The anonymous first opinion asks for rain from the 3rd of Marheshvan. Rabban Gamliel says the 7th, fifteen days after the festival, so that the last Israelite pilgrim can reach the Euphrates. The Yerushalmi's own halakhah on that Mishnah (1:3:2) calls the anonymous opinion R. Meir's, and gives a ruling 'in the name of R. Hoshaya' that follows the 3rd.

evidence.exact_quote: בִּשְׁלשָׁה בְּמַרְחֶשְׁוָן שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים. רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר בְּשִׁבְעָה בוֹ חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר יוֹם אַחַר הֶחָג כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ הָאַחֲרוֹן שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לִנְהַר פְּרָת.

ontology_lessons: A kinship epithet in the printed text ('אחוי') can conflict with a kinship term in the same sentence ('חביבך'). The graph needs a way to store an explicit-but-emended reading without asserting it.
Parallel passages with the same framing formula (JT Taanit 1:2:4 and JT Megillah 3:7:3) are strong evidence for a text reading. They are not evidence that the same event is meant.

A verb's construal can decide whether a person takes part in an exchange at all (את מציית 'you pressed/heard' vs אתמציית 'it became clear to him'). Claims should be able to branch on the reading, not just on the referent.

Separate three kinds of voice: the anonymous Talmud voice (challenger), the anonymous Mishnah voice (the 3rd-of-Marheshvan opinion), and attributions the Talmud itself makes ('this is R. Meir's Mishnah'). None should become a person node by default.
A precedent spoken inside an attributed view ('שכן מצאנו ... בימי יואל') is an attributed exegetical claim. A biblical name used as a time anchor is not a relationship partner.
Commentators often mark conjectures with 'אפשר' or 'כנראה', and a lexicon may mark one with 'prob.'. Keep these hedges as a separate confidence basis from lexical or textual evidence.
Shared patronymics across Talmuds (Yehuda vs Yehoshua ben Betera) and shared names within one chapter (several R. Hoshaya and R. Yose mentions) must not merge automatically.
When commentary consensus resolves a pronoun (בעון קומוי → R. Yohanan), record the basis as commentary consensus plus internal evidence, distinct from 'explicit'.
